Part I: Repository and workflow

Part II: Web scraping

Question 1: Scrape a table

```{r}
library(rvest)
library(dplyr)
library(janitor)
library(readr)
library(purrr)
```

Read the Wikipedia page on Chicago community areas into R
```{r}
ca_page <- read_html("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_areas_in_Chicago")
```

This page consists of more than one table, so I'll grab akk the data tables ("wikitable")
```{r}
ca_tables <- ca_page |>
  html_elements("table.wikitable") |>
  html_table()
```

The number of tables we found
```{r}
length(ca_tables)
```

Keeping the table that has a "Total Population" column (the one that lists every community area and its population)
```{r}
ca_raw <- ca_tables |>
  keep(~ "Total Population" %in% names(.x)) |>
  pluck(1)

nrow(ca_raw)
head(ca_raw)
```
Question 2: Scrape with CSS selectors
Question 2.1. Extract title, price and availability

Reading the books' first page to scrape
```{r}
books_page <- read_html("https://books.toscrape.com/")
```

Each book is inside <article class="product_pod">
Full title is in the "title" attribute of the link inside <h3> (visible text is cut off for long titles)
```{r}
title <- books_page |>
  html_elements("article.product_pod h3 a") |>
  html_attr("title")
```

Price is the text of <p class="price_color">
```{r}
price <- books_page |>
  html_elements("article.product_pod p.price_color") |>
  html_text2()
```

Availability is the text of <p class="instock availability">
```{r}
availability <- books_page |>
  html_elements("article.product_pod p.instock.availability") |>
  html_text2()
```

Now, I have to combine the three vectors into one table
```{r}
books <- tibble(title, price, availability)

nrow(books)
head(books)
```

Question 2.2 Numeric price and save to CSV
```{r}
books <- books |>
  mutate(price = round(parse_number(price), 2))

nrow(books)
head(books)
```

Save the table as books.csv
```{r}
write_csv(books, "books.csv")
```

BONUS
The rating is stored as a class name, e.g. <p class="star-rating Three">. Pulling the class and dropping "star-rating", and mapping the word to a number 1-5
```{r}
library(stringr)
```


```{r}
rating_word <- books_page |>
  html_elements("article.product_pod p.star-rating") |>
  html_attr("class") |>
  str_remove("star-rating ")

books <- books |>
  mutate(rating = recode(rating_word,
                         One = 1, Two = 2, Three = 3, Four = 4, Five = 5))

nrow(books)
head(books)
```

Saving the CSV file again, so it includes the rating column
```{r}
write_csv(books, "books.csv")
```


Part III: Open data API (Chicago Data Portal)

1. Request the data
```{r}
library(httr)
library(jsonlite)
library(dplyr)

# Chicago Data Portal endpoint for 311 service requests (no API key needed)
sr_url <- "https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/v6vf-nfxy.json"

# Query parameters:
# - community_area "24" keeps only West Town (written as text)
# - $where keeps requests created on or after Jan 1, 2026
# - $order puts the newest requests first
# - $limit caps the result at 1,000 rows

sr_query <- list(
  community_area = "24",
  `$where` = "created_date >= '2026-01-01T00:00:00'",
  `$order` = "created_date DESC",
  `$limit` = 1000
)

# Send the GET request with those parameters
sr_response <- GET(sr_url, query = sr_query)

# A status code of 200 means the request worked
status_code(sr_response)
```
2. Parse the response

```{r}
# Pull the body of the response out as text, then turn the JSON into a data frame.
# flatten = TRUE spreads nested fields (like location) into regular columns
sr_text <- content(sr_response, as = "text", encoding = "UTF-8")
west_town_311 <- fromJSON(sr_text, flatten = TRUE)

# Number of rows (should be 1,000) and the column names
nrow(west_town_311)
names(west_town_311)
```

3. Summarize
```{r}
# Count how many requests there are of each type,
# sort from most to least common, and keep the top 10
west_town_311 |>
  count(sr_type, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

4. Interpretation
The top request was graffiti removal (200/1,000, roughly 1 in 5). It was followed by rat complaints, parking enforcement reviews, yard waste pick-up, potholes, sign repair, and street lights out. Majority of the requests are about keeping the neighbourhood clean, which suggests that residents of West Town mainly rely on 311 for everyday cleanup of streets and public spaces. Though, the data can't tell whether the problem got fixed or how well. About half of the requests were still open.  

Part IV: Census API (tidycensus)

Step 1: Identify the variables

| Variable | Code |
|---|---|
| Gross rent as % of household income, Total | B25070_001E |
| Gross rent as % of household income, 50.0 percent or more | **B25070_010E** |
| Median household income | **B19013_001E** |

I found B25070_010E by browsing the B25070 group, and B19013_001E by browsing the B19013 group
(Median Household Income in the Past 12 Months).

Step 2: Retrieve the data

```{r}
# Load tidycensus (Census API) and tidyverse (dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2)
# The API key is read from .Renviron, so it never appears in this file
library(tidycensus)
library(tidyverse)

# Get the three variables for every county in Ohio from the 2024 ACS 5-year.
# Naming the variables here gives readable names instead of codes
ohio_raw <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  state = "OH",
  variables = c(rent_total    = "B25070_001",
                rent_50plus   = "B25070_010",
                median_income = "B19013_001"),
  year = 2024,
  survey = "acs5"
)

# Long format: 3 rows per county (88 counties x 3 = 264 rows)
nrow(ohio_raw)
head(ohio_raw)
```

Step 3: Clean and transform
```{r}
# 1. Drop the margin of error, then pivot so each county is one row
#    with the three estimates side by side
# 2. severe_burden_rate = share of renter households paying 50%+ of income on rent
# 3. Sort from highest to lowest rate
ohio <- ohio_raw |>
  select(GEOID, NAME, variable, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = estimate) |>
  mutate(severe_burden_rate = rent_50plus / rent_total * 100) |>
  arrange(desc(severe_burden_rate))

nrow(ohio)
head(ohio)
```

Bonus: Split NAME into county and state

```{r p4-bonus}
# NAME looks like "Athens County, Ohio" -- split it at ", " into two columns
ohio <- ohio |>
  separate_wider_delim(NAME, delim = ", ", names = c("county", "state"))

head(ohio)
```

Step 4: Analyze
```{r}
# Mean and median severe burden rate across Ohio's 88 counties
ohio |>
  summarise(mean_rate   = mean(severe_burden_rate),
            median_rate = median(severe_burden_rate))

# The 5 counties with the highest rates
top5 <- ohio |>
  slice_max(severe_burden_rate, n = 5) |>
  select(county, severe_burden_rate, median_income)
top5

# The 5 counties with the lowest rates
bottom5 <- ohio |>
  slice_min(severe_burden_rate, n = 5) |>
  select(county, severe_burden_rate, median_income)
bottom5
```
